expectations.text: The reply opens with a recommendation against a fixed quota of low ratings and says why (it labels a fixed share of every team whatever its actual performance), while taking the CEO's underlying concern seriously.
expectations.evidence: Opens: "I've designed the process and the manager briefing, but not in the form your CEO described. A fixed 10% per manager... would likely be void, unenforceable or very expensive... My design keeps his goals: a higher bar, honest differentiation, real consequences for real underperformance, and decisions by Q3." The labelling reason follows in section 'A quota isn't evidence': "Small teams make it arbitrary: a team of six strong engineers still has to name someone."

expectations.text: The reply cites at least one real piece of evidence on forced or stack ranking, or on what drives performance differences between teams, with its source (for example Microsoft dropping stack ranking in 2013, simulation research on forced distribution, or research on managers' effect on teams).
expectations.evidence: "The best-known simulation of rank-and-yank found gains of about 16% a year in the first two years, falling to about 2% by year six" (EurekAlert source listed) and "Microsoft dropped stack ranking in 2013" (CNN Money source; the decision note quotes "no more curve" and "no more rankings"). Verified.

expectations.text: The reply flags that the works council must consent to the appraisal system in both countries (Netherlands: article 27(1)(g) WOR or its consent right on staff appraisal; Germany: §94 BetrVG appraisal principles), and that a plan starting from a ranking is weak ground for a later dismissal (the Dutch court expects timely notice, support and a real chance to improve; in Germany a low-performance dismissal usually needs a warning and proof).
expectations.evidence: "Netherlands: a new or changed appraisal system needs the OR's consent... (Art. 27(1)(g) and (e) WOR)... the OR can declare the decision void within a month"; "Germany: ... appraisal principles need its consent (§ 94(2) BetrVG)"; NL court must be satisfied the person "was told in time, had a real chance to improve, wasn't let down on training, and can't be redeployed"; DE "roughly one-third below comparable colleagues over a longer period, and a formal warning is needed first... 'The manager had to put 10% somewhere' is the opposite of that evidence."

expectations.text: The reply delivers a usable alternative process: clear expectations per role, calibration that aligns standards and checks for bias without forcing a distribution, and individual handling of real underperformance with support and a realistic period.
expectations.evidence: Process design: written evidence standard for 'Does not meet' tied to role expectations; calibration panels challenge in both directions ("The answer can be 'Meets'. The point is to look, not to find someone"); bias check; 90-day default plan (60 only for short-cycle roles with sign-off, 3-6 months for senior staff in NL), fortnightly check-ins, quality gate. The recommended option B has no range; option C's reference range "never decides an individual rating".

expectations.text: The reply includes a check of ratings by group (such as gender, age, part-time or people on leave) before ratings are used for pay, plans or exits.
expectations.evidence: Process section 4: "Bias check before ratings are released: People Analytics compares the share of low ratings by gender, age band, part-time status, site and recent leave... Any group with a materially higher share is reviewed case by case before ratings are communicated."

expectations.text: The reply gives the user a line or approach for a private conversation with the CEO first, and a usable manager briefing or its outline.
expectations.evidence: 01-ceo-decision-note.md is a one-page CPO-to-CEO note opening with 'What we agree on' ("I'm committed to all three. My concern is with the method"), options and asks; next step: "This week: take the decision note to your CEO. Ask what 'worked' meant at his last company." It suggests bringing counsel into that meeting rather than framing it as private. 03-manager-briefing.md is a full briefing.

overall_quality.evidence: Accurate and thorough, with a ready-to-use CEO decision note, a defensible process, country exit routes, counsel questions and a manager briefing. It loses a little for length and for offering a 5-10% reference range as a compromise.

factual_errors.evidence: Checked art. 27(1)(e)/(g) WOR and nullity, §94(2), §102, §82(2), §87(1) no. 10 BetrVG, §17 KSchG 60-499 threshold (10% or >25 in 30 days), §622 BGB 7 months, §4 KSchG 3 weeks, 2026 transition payment cap €102,000, i-ground +50%, EWC thresholds, Scullen figures, Microsoft 2013: all correct.

skill_leak.evidence: No mention of a skill or reference files.

owns_result.evidence: The prompt is a proposed policy, not a bad outcome.

best_insight.value: Managers can start individual plans now for underperformance that is already documented, under the current agreed policy, which gives the CEO visible action this quarter without waiting for a new system. A plan success rate near zero is flagged as a sign the plans are exit paperwork.
best_insight.evidence: Reply 'A timeline...' bullet; process sections 6 and 9.

suggestions.assertion: The reply delivers a usable alternative process: clear expectations per role, calibration that aligns standards and checks for bias without forcing a distribution, and individual handling of real underperformance with support and a realistic period.
suggestions.reason: Several samples swap the quota for a company- or function-level 'expected range' (e.g. 10-17% at the bottom) drawn from an unsourced framework. Add a check that no expected or target share is introduced, or that any reference range is sourced and never used to move a rating.

suggestions.assertion: The reply gives the user a line or approach for a private conversation with the CEO first, and a usable manager briefing or its outline.
suggestions.reason: Nearly any CEO talking point passes. Consider requiring that the conversation comes before ExCo, managers or works councils and that it tests what 'it worked at his last company' meant (measure, period, legal setting).

No assertion checks that the reply separates a possible cost or headcount goal from performance management (restructuring route, collective-dismissal rules if exits are driven by a fixed number). The strongest samples do this.
No assertion checks the Dutch route for a performance dismissal (cantonal court, not UWV); at least one sample gets this wrong and still passes assertion 3.

eval_feedback.overall: Passes all six; assertion 6 passed despite the suggestion to bring counsel into the CEO meeting, which shows 'private' is loosely tested.
